extracted.intended_audience: parties and practitioners in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards applied by the PTAB when deciding whether to institute an inter partes review under 35 U.S.C. § 314 and related discretionary-denial analyses (§ 314(a), § 325(d)), claim construction, and obviousness evaluation at the institution stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review may not be instituted unless the information presented in the Petition and any preliminary response shows that 'there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a preliminary standard (not a final determination). If instituted, the Board must address all grounds of unpatentability raised in the petition (see SAS Inst., Inc. v. Iancu and AC Techs. S.A. v. Amazon.com, Inc.). Institution requires a showing of reasonable likelihood for at least one challenged claim on the current record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factors for discretionary denial under § 314(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six non-exclusive factors to determine 'whether efficiency, fairness, and the merits support the exercise of authority to deny institution in view of an earlier trial date in the parallel proceeding.' The factors are: (1) whether the court granted a stay or evidence exists that one may be granted; (2) proximity of the court’s trial date to the Board’s projected statutory deadline for a final written decision; (3) investment in the parallel proceeding by the court and the parties; (4) overlap between issues raised in the petition and in the parallel proceeding; (5) whether the petitioner and the defendant in the parallel proceeding are the same party; and (6) other circumstances that impact the Board’s exercise of discretion, including the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fintiv factors are non-exclusive, part of a balanced assessment, and should be applied in view of Director guidance (Guidance Memo), CTPG, and precedent (AviaGames, Volvo Penta). An early trial date is only one part of the assessment. The Board considers the merits (the 'compelling merits' standard) only if the first five factors favor denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to apply 'compelling merits' in Fintiv analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board should consider whether the record prior to institution demonstrates that the merits are compelling only if the first five Fintiv factors favor exercising discretion to deny institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Director remands (AviaGames, Volvo Penta): do a Fintiv analysis; only if factors 1–5 favor denial should the Board consider whether merits are compelling. The Director has cautioned not to deny institution based solely on a district court § 101 judgment when the record shows compelling merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 325(d) two‑part framework (Advanced Bionics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-part test for denying institution under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d): (1) whether the same or substantially the same art previously was presented to the Office or whether the same or substantially the same arguments previously were presented to the Office; and (2) if so, whether the petitioner has demonstrated that the Office erred in a manner material to the patentability of challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Advanced Bionics framework and use Becton, Dickinson factors for assessing part (1). Previously presented art includes art of record by the Examiner and art provided in IDS/prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becton, Dickinson factor considerations for § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors useful for applying Advanced Bionics: (a) the similarities and material differences between the asserted art and the prior art involved during examination; (b) the cumulative nature of the asserted art and the prior art evaluated during examination; and (d) the extent of the overlap between the arguments made during examination and the manner in which Petitioner relies on the prior art or Patent Owner distinguishes the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors to determine whether the same or substantially the same art/arguments were previously presented. If satisfied, proceed to evaluate whether the petitioner shows material error by the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) (Graham/KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 103(a) forbids issuance of a patent when 'the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious' to a person having ordinary skill in the art. The obviousness inquiry involves underlying factual determinations including: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and when presented, (4) objective evidence of non‑obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Graham factors and KSR precedent. Evaluate combination teachings (e.g., Wu + Doherty) in light of what a POSITA would find routine or predictable, and include consideration of any objective indicia if presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors for determining a POSITA include the types of problems encountered in the art, the sophistication of the technology, and the educational level of active workers in the field. One or more factors may predominate. Education and experience can be substitutable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board adopts a POSITA definition consistent with the record (e.g., petitioner’s expert declaration). Use the POSITA to interpret claim terms and to assess obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips/district-court-type; 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In IPRs, the Board interprets claim language using the district-court-type standard described in Phillips: claim terms have their ordinary and customary meaning to a POSITA at the time of invention, in light of the claim language, the specification, and the prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on intrinsic evidence first (claims, spec, prosecution history). Parties may propose constructions but Board need only construe disputed terms as necessary to resolve institution/trial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit constructions to terms 'in controversy' and 'to the extent necessary' (Nidec/Vivid)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board (and courts) need only construe terms that are in controversy, and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary claim construction at institution; construe additional terms later if needed for trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from preferred embodiments (Liebel‑Flarsheim)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to read limitations from a preferred embodiment described in the specification into the claims absent a clear indication in the intrinsic record that the patentee intended the claims to be so limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be narrowed to particular examples in the specification unless the specification clearly and unambiguously requires that limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reluctance to read negative limitations without express disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board (and Federal Circuit) are reluctant to read a written description to affirmatively exclude or disclaim an element absent an express statement to that effect; to import a negative limitation the specification must convey that the inventor intended the exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Healthier Choices Mgmt. Corp. v. Philip Morris Prods. S.A. and Novartis v. Accord Healthcare: negative limitations generally require express language or clear conveyance to skilled artisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as 'previously presented art' for § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously presented art includes art made of record by the Examiner and art provided to the Office by an applicant (for example, on an Information Disclosure Statement) in the prosecution history of the challenged patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing § 325(d), compare the asserted references and arguments to the prosecution record and prior Office analyses to determine substantial sameness or cumulative nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of overlap with parallel district court proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a parallel district court proceeding exists (including district-court judgments such as § 101 rulings), the Board should assess staying, proximity of trial dates, investment by the court/parties, issue overlap, party identity, and other circumstances (Fintiv factors) in deciding whether to exercise discretion to deny institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director guidance (AviaGames, Volvo Penta) explains that a district court § 101 judgment does not automatically justify denial; if the Board reaches that Fintiv factors 1–5 favor denial, it must then consider whether the merits are compelling. Consider appeal/remand possibilities and potential statutory bars (e.g., § 315(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary-record sufficiency and the role of the Institution Decision
rubrics_metrics.description: An Institution Decision assesses the petition on the current preliminary record and determines whether there is a reasonable likelihood of prevailing on at least one claim; it is not a final decision on patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board's institution determination is based on the petition, preliminary response, and associated evidence/declarations. Institution triggers the trial timeline but does not resolve ultimate patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific example of claim-meaning guidance (interpretation of 'change a predetermined advertisement insertion point')
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of this proceeding, the limitation 'change a predetermined advertisement insertion point ... in response to receiving a user input to update a current play position to a new play position' at least includes skipping over a predetermined ad insertion point to ultimately arrive at a different ad insertion point in response to the user activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims in light of the specification and prosecution history but do not limit claims to a single example; the Board explained that the specification contemplates placing ad blocks between tracks or immediately before resuming play after a user-directed skip, and that limitation 1.e includes skipping over an insertion point to a different insertion point.
